\chapter{No Hables --- Telling Somebody Not To}
\label{ch:command-negative}
\hlchaptermodality{124}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give a negative informal command, and say why it takes the subjunctive.}

Complete ES-C50-no-hables: produce no hables and say why the subjunctive is the right form.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[no hables]{no hables — telling somebody not to}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-no-hables}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Speak\textquotedblright{} is \emph{habla}. So \textquotedblleft{}don't speak\textquotedblright{} should be \emph{no habla}. Say it, and then be told it is wrong.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the form you already learned for wanting}]
\begin{quote}
A \textbf{negative} command uses the \textbf{subjunctive}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{no \textbf{hables}} — don't speak. \emph{no \textbf{comas}} — don't eat.
\end{quote}

Those are not new forms. You built them chapters ago, when you learned to say \emph{quiero que hables} — \textquotedblleft{}I want you to speak.\textquotedblright{}

And the connection is not an accident of grammar. Think about what the subjunctive was \textbf{for}: the form for something \textbf{not asserted} — wanted, feared, hoped for, but not claimed to be happening.

A negative command is exactly that. \emph{No hables} does not describe any speaking. There is no speaking; the whole point of the sentence is that you want there to be none. Spanish reaches for the non-asserting form because nothing is being asserted.

So this is not \textquotedblleft{}the negative command borrows the subjunctive.\textquotedblright{} It is the subjunctive doing the thing it has always done.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
There is a lopsidedness here worth naming, because it looks like untidiness and is not.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{habla} — an ordinary present form. \textbf{no hables} — a subjunctive form.
\end{quote}

Two different shapes for one verb, depending only on whether there is a \emph{no} in front. Most languages would use one form for both.

The reason Spanish does not is that the two sentences are doing genuinely different things. \emph{Habla} points at an action and hands it to you. \emph{No hables} points at an action \textbf{and refuses it} — and the refusal, not the action, is the sentence's content. The form follows the content, as it did in every subjunctive sentence you have already met.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habla\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}no hables\textquotedblright{} — hear the form change with the no
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quiero que hables\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}no hables\textquotedblright{} — the same form, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}Don't speak\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{No hables}}.) Which form is that? (The \textbf{subjunctive} — the one for what is not asserted.) Next: the same form again, this time for politeness rather than negation.
\end{tcolorbox}
